1.pericope_label: Jesus, full of the Spirit, is led into the wilderness and tempted to command the stone

schools.summary: Read the order of events as a warning that baptism is followed by temptation; and follow the phrase about fulness of the Spirit forward to the deacons and to Stephen rather than into the wilderness.

Give three reasons for the wilderness — to provoke the adversary, to recover in a mystery the Adam driven out of Paradise, and to show by example that the devil envies every attempt at better things; and explain the hunger as a nature voluntarily assumed, the Lord being untempted through the forty days because the devil dared not approach one who fasted without hungering.
State the conflict as substitution: he took the form of a slave and stood as our avenger against the serpent, so that we might conquer in him where we fell in Adam.
Take the genealogy that closes the previous chapter as the ground of this one — the Son of Adam is the seed of the woman, and here at the opening of the war he conquers the conqueror.
Keep the received punctuation against the versions that put the forty days before the tempting, and allow that Satan may have tempted him invisibly, by internal suggestion, before appearing openly.

Deny that the temptations proper began before the forty days were over; press the continuous force of the verb and the double mention of the Spirit; note that Luke’s singular “this stone” is more vivid than Matthew’s plural; and suppose the leading into the wilderness may have been a literal carrying through the air, the devil perhaps imitating it to claim the worship due to the Spirit.

Set the three evangelists’ verbs side by side and insist that all three assign the leading to the Spirit and not to Satan, so that the forty days are forty days of being sustained; and canvass the site of the wilderness.

debates: Whether the temptation ran through the forty days or began only at their end — Basil and Barnes say the devil did not approach until the fast was over, while Gill keeps the received reading and posits invisible temptation throughout.
How Jesus was brought into the wilderness: by inward impulse, or, as Lightfoot conjectures, by being physically caught up through the air as Philip was.
Why the wilderness was chosen — to provoke the adversary, to reverse Adam’s expulsion, or to exemplify the devil’s envy of every advance (all three given by Ambrose).
Whether Luke’s singular “this stone” differs materially from Matthew’s plural, which Ellicott and Robertson both press.
outliers: Lightfoot alone takes the leading into the wilderness for a bodily translation through the air, and alone suggests the devil counterfeited it.
Basil alone explains why the devil waited, and alone reads the hunger as a deliberate provocation rather than a weakness.
Clarke alone turns the three verbs into a pastoral rule for the tempted.
Robertson alone raises the question of where the narrative could have come from, and answers that it could only have come from Christ.

5.pericope_label: The kingdoms of the world shown in a moment, and the demand for worship

schools.summary: Hold, against those who make the vision imaginary, that the kingdoms were shown in visible form; and answer the tempter’s claim over gold and silver with the prophet’s words that they are God’s to give, adding that money itself may open the kingdom of heaven.

Weigh the word for “moment” and the word for “world”; account for the vision as mental or as the ecstatic compression of images; describe rather than adjudicate the two evangelists’ orders, one geographical and one climactic; and divide over the tempter’s claim to hold the kingdoms, one voice calling it a lying boast without scriptural foundation and the other noting that Jesus does not deny it.

Prefer Matthew’s order as the true one that Luke neglects without contradicting; and contrast the good angel, who refuses worship and directs men to God, with the fallen one who sought it from the Son of God and fell by that very ambition.

Hold that this temptation stands last in Matthew and that Luke gives the particulars out of sequence; and contradict the tempter outright, since it is God who puts down one and sets up another, though Satan by permission may cause great revolutions.
Distinguish power, which is from God, from the lust of power, which is from the evil one, and press the irony that a man must serve in order to rule.

debates: Whether the kingdoms were shown to the eye (Theophylact), to the imagination (Robertson), or in an ecstatic compression of images (Ellicott).
Which evangelist gives the true order of the temptations — Matthew, on the evidence of his connecting words (Gill, Clarke), or neither, both orders being schemes of their own (Robertson).
Whether the tempter’s claim to have received the kingdoms was a lie with no scriptural basis (Ellicott) or a claim Jesus pointedly left unchallenged (Robertson).
What acceptance would have amounted to: a recognition of authority rather than merit, and rule by bargain instead of by conquest (Robertson).
outliers: Theophylact alone states a positive view on the mode of the vision against the commoner one.
Lightfoot alone quotes a rabbinic measurement of a “moment”, and alone mocks its precision.
Cyril of Jerusalem alone answers the tempter by quoting the verse his offer parodies.
Ambrose alone turns the temptation into an argument about the cost of holding office.

9.pericope_label: Set on the pinnacle: cast thyself down, for it is written

schools.summary: Identify the third weapon as boasting, which throws down those who glory in their own good deeds, and hold that the devil can injure no one who has not first thrown himself down; read his withdrawal as the retreat of a beaten enemy who dreads a second defeat and will return to fight openly rather than to tempt; and hold, on the order of the temptations, that it is uncertain and does not matter, provided all of them happened.

Make Christ the willing wrestler who invites the contest; deny that the devil ever contended with God, since he did not dare and said “if thou art the Son of God”, his quarrel being with the man he had once deceived; and explain the season of his departure as filled with a subtler assault, the stirring up of enemies so that love itself might be broken — while accounting for the evangelists’ different orders by the way vain-glory and covetousness beget each other.
Report the older observation that the tempter dropped the middle clause of the psalm he quoted, and suggest that this journey too may have been made through the air.

Insist that the psalm is not misquoted but misapplied, made to mean presumptuous reliance on God, and note the clause Luke adds to the quotation and the uncertainty about what the wing of the temple was.

debates: Whom the tempter took himself to be contending with — God, or the man he had deceived before, which Athanasius settles from the conditional “if thou art the Son of God”.
What the “season” of the devil’s departure covers: the interval before open warfare (Ambrose) or a continued and subtler campaign through human enemies (Maximus).
Whether the difference of order between the evangelists can or need be resolved — Augustine says it cannot and does not matter, Maximus explains why either order is natural.
Whether the tempter misquoted the psalm or only misapplied it, and what to make of the clause he omitted (Robertson, Gill).
outliers: Ambrose alone makes the devil’s weakness the point, that he can hurt no one who has not first cast himself down.
Origen alone has Christ inviting the contest in the tempter’s hearing.
Maximus alone treats the whole later ministry as the continuation of this temptation by other means.
Gill alone reports that the omitted clause of the psalm was noticed as early as Jerome.

12.pericope_label: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God; and the devil departed for a season

schools.summary: Note that Luke’s formula of citation differs from Matthew’s and that all three answers come from one book; explain the number of the trials as a complete cycle of what human nature was then open to, or as exhausting appetite, nerve and ambition; identify the returning season with the Passion, the tempter changing from allurement to suffering; and draw from the silence about later temptations the assurance that a way of escape is always made.

Take “all the temptation” as widely as possible, covering the invisible and inward assaults of the whole forty days as well as the three recorded, and gather the versions that describe how completely and how vainly the devil spent his strength.
Name the convenient season outright as the garden of Gethsemane.

debates: Whether the tempting ran through the forty days, with the three trials standing for the whole (Gill, and Robertson), or whether the three are the complete and only cycle (Ellicott).

What the “season” of return was — Gethsemane (Wesley), the hour of the power of darkness at the close (Ellicott), a series of recurring opportunities of which Gethsemane was the worst (Robertson), or the whole later campaign conducted through human instruments (Lightfoot).
Why nothing is recorded of the later temptations, which Barnes turns from a difficulty into a promise.
outliers: Lightfoot alone explains the departure as a change of method forced on the tempter by failure.
Ellicott alone argues that three trials are exactly the number human nature then admitted.
Robertson alone compares the severity of this assault with the one in Gethsemane, and ranks the later one higher.
Barnes alone converts the silence of the record into a general assurance for the tempted.

14.pericope_label: Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit and teaches in their synagogues

schools.summary: Divide over what the power means — one voice allowing that power was added, but only as regards its manifestation, the other denying any addition and grounding the miracles in the Son’s own nature and possession of all that is the Father’s, so that the grace of the Spirit is exercised as his own.

Describe the change as a new phase of life in which latent powers were developed, and mark the chapters of another Gospel that belong in the gap; set out the three characteristics of the Galilean ministry and the force of the words for power and for fame; and read the general admiration as the habit of a season before hostility was roused.

Identify the Spirit of the ministry with the Spirit of the wilderness and compare a Targum’s phrase for being filled with the spirit of prophecy; and hold that the admiration is recorded to show that a divine power shone in Christ from the very commencement, compelling even the malignant to admire.

Take the return as an abundant strengthening after conflict and make the whole episode a rule, that grace turns what was designed for our ruin into our greatest good; and use the open synagogue to ask whether an unconforming preacher would be admitted to the pulpits of an established church.
Count the choice of a remote province part of the humiliation, and observe that Christ waited for no call from men, having light and life in himself.

debates: Whether anything was added to Christ at all — Origen allows an addition in the manifestation only, Cyril denies any addition and grounds the power in his nature.

What the phrase marks: a change of phase comparable to Pentecost with latent powers developed (Ellicott), a strengthening after conflict (Wesley), or continuity with the Spirit of the wilderness (Gill).

Why the general admiration is recorded — as evidence of a divine power visible from the first (Calvin), as the habit of a period before opposition (Robertson), or as the calm before it (Ellicott, Wesley).
outliers: Cyril alone refuses the language of added power and argues the point christologically.
Clarke alone turns the freedom of the synagogues into a question about the churches of his own day.
Robertson alone lays out the ministry under three heads and traces the etymologies that carry them.
Henry alone treats the obscurity of the province as part of the humiliation.

16.pericope_label: At Nazareth he reads Isaiah and says: this day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears

schools.summary: Draw from Christ’s regular attendance the duty of public worship even where doctrine is impure; set out the order of the synagogue service and the state of the rolls; infer from the handing of the roll that the passage was the appointed lesson; note that the text read follows the Greek version and includes a clause absent from the Hebrew; and rebuke the fathers who inferred a one-year ministry from the word “year”.

Deny that the passage was appointed and hold that Christ deliberately chose it, a liberty of choice being allowed him; make the time of redemption depend on God’s good pleasure against minds impatient of delay; explain the congregation’s fixed attention as an astonishment God sent to keep them from interrupting; and note that the Spirit was given to Christ as man without measure.

Hold that better worship is attended imperfectly than not at all; state the rule that the Jews read standing and preached sitting; take the finding of the place as a particular providence rather than a lesson or a choice; and observe that a second prophetic passage is joined to the first in the reading.
Use the name of the town as a prophecy that binds Christ to the Creator, and therefore against a Christ who should have avoided the Creator’s places.
Follow the opening clause about the Spirit not into the sermon but into the Acts, as evidence that the Spirit speaks, separates, calls and sends with authority.

debates: Whether the passage was the appointed lesson for the day (Ellicott, Clarke), deliberately chosen by Christ (Calvin), or opened on by particular providence (Wesley).
Whether Isaiah was a separate roll — Lightfoot leaves it open, Barnes infers that the books were kept apart, Ellicott says it is clear.
Whether the word “year” fixes the length of the ministry, which Ellicott and Robertson both deny and blame on a slavish literalism among the fathers.
What sitting down signified, which Ellicott says means the opposite to a Jewish reader from what it suggests to a modern one.
outliers: Lightfoot alone supplies the rabbinic rules about standing and leaning to read.
Calvin alone denies that the lectionary settled the text and insists on a deliberate choice.
Tertullian alone reads the place-name as a prophecy and turns it into a polemical argument.
Ellicott alone reconstructs why the claim startled hearers who had known the family.

22.pericope_label: The gracious words, the proverb of the physician, and the examples of Elijah and Elisha

schools.summary: Distinguish assent to the exposition from faith in the expositor, and hold that they acknowledged God speaking in Christ while refusing him the honour; and explain the absence of miracles as a withholding, since unbelief cannot bind God’s hands but does forfeit the benefit of his works.

Trace the history of the word “grace” through the New Testament; note that the physician’s proverb stands in the physician’s Gospel and appears in Greek and Latin authors as well as Jewish; deny that it reflects on Christ’s own condition; read the two Old Testament examples as a specimen of Christ’s way of finding the underlying lesson of a narrative, and explain why they gave a double offence; and account for the three and a half years as popular reckoning.
Explain the absence of miracles as a refusal to provoke greater malice, the teaching being set before them instead; and take the formula of asseveration as a way into the question of eternal life.

Explain the slight by the common failing that what is always at hand is despised; notice that no Capernaum miracle has yet been narrated and infer a concealed mystery, Nazareth standing for the Jews and Capernaum for the Gentiles; and allegorise the widow as the soul bereft of virtue that learns to feed on the word.
Make the withdrawal of miracles a judgement on envy, a country proving unworthy of its citizen’s works which had been worthy of the Son of God’s conception.

Ascribe the want of miracles to unbelief; complain that no evangelist preserved the sermon and infer that it cannot have been necessary to salvation; reconcile the three and a half years by reckoning the third year from the arrival at Sarepta; and state the rule that justice follows fixed rules while beneficence is free.

debates: What the congregation actually conceded — the correctness of the exposition only (Gill) or the messianic claim itself (Barnes), with Calvin holding that they granted the divine power and refused the honour.

Why no miracle was wrought at Nazareth: to avoid provoking malice (Chrysostom), as a judgement on envy (Ambrose), because familiarity breeds contempt (Cyril), or because unbelief forfeits the benefit (Calvin, Wesley).

How to reconcile the three years and six months with the third year of the Kings narrative — literally with an admitted difficulty (Lightfoot), by shifting the terminus to Sarepta (Wesley), or by treating the figure as popular idiom (Robertson).
Whether the reference to Capernaum can stand where no Capernaum miracle has been reported, which Origen resolves by allegory.
outliers: Origen alone treats the narrative difficulty as the door to a typology of Jew and Gentile.
Ellicott alone wonders whether the physician’s proverb is what drew the physician-evangelist to this history.
Lightfoot alone explains the double offence the two examples gave.
Clarke alone turns the episode into a general distinction between justice, which is bound by rules, and beneficence, which is free.

28.pericope_label: The rage of the synagogue, the brow of the hill, and the passing through the midst

schools.summary: Take the offence to be that he seemed to rank himself with the prophets.

Enumerate the grounds of the anger, from insulted town pride to the fear of being ranked below Gentiles; deny that the town had any legal power over life and note that this manner of killing was no recognised Jewish penalty; and set the traditional site of the precipice against a nearer cliff that fits the narrative better.
State the inference they drew and concede that it was near the truth, the kingdom being in fact taken from them for forfeited privilege; and report a traveller’s account of the traditional precipice.

Observe that conviction turned to madness rather than to repentance, and canvass how the escape was made — speed, another form, invisibility, or holding their eyes — concluding that he who could do this then laid down his life freely afterwards.
Find both natures in the escape, the standing unseized betokening divinity and the departure declaring the incarnation.

Insist that the endurance was voluntary, since he is taken when he wills and escapes when he wills; and give three reasons why this was not the appointed death — the hour, the place, and the manner all being other.

debates: Why the congregation turned — because he seemed to rank himself with the prophets (Cyril), because Gentile faith was preferred to theirs (Ellicott, Barnes), or because local pride was affronted (Robertson).
Whether the inference they drew was false: Clarke concedes it was near the truth and explains why the privileges were forfeited.
How the escape was effected, and whether it was miraculous — Gill lists four possibilities, while Chrysostom and Ambrose make it a display of the two natures and of voluntary endurance.
Where the precipice was, the traditional Mount of Precipitation being reported by Barnes and Clarke and rejected by Ellicott as too distant.
outliers: Clarke alone grants that the enraged hearers had read his meaning correctly.
Bede alone gives reasons drawn from the hour, the place and the manner of the appointed death.
Lightfoot alone asks what legal authority the town could have claimed, and raises the licence of the zealots.
Ellicott alone disputes the traditional site and proposes another.

31.pericope_label: At Capernaum: teaching with authority, and the unclean spirit cast out

schools.summary: Deny that the move was made in resentment and make it an act of mercy to an unbelieving people; find the sabbath significant, the new creation beginning where the old ceased and the Son of God shown to be above the Law; state that a teacher’s word has power only when his actions match it; refuse to be shocked that a devil first names Jesus in this Gospel; and turn Marcion’s dating of the descent to Capernaum into an absurdity.

Make the visit the act of a physician to the mortally sick who taught them openly; explain that miracles are mingled with teaching to rouse those whose reason does not incline to knowledge; and account for the devils’ cry by the later charge that Christ cast out devils by Beelzebub.

Read the devil’s confession as an attempt to disturb the order of things and to take from the Apostles the dignity of confessing Christ; and follow the exorcism forward into the Acts, where the same power drives out unclean spirits.

Note the distance and the descent from the hill town; read the phrase about the spirit as meaning that the man was driven by the devil’s impulse, his faculties seized; and take the general amazement as a forced acknowledgment that traces the miracle to the doctrine.

Observe that Luke alone gives the reason for the removal and that he here follows the other evangelist; weigh the unique phrase for the spirit against the usage of the other Gospels and consider whether it points to a necromantic spirit; and mark what Luke alone records — that the man took no hurt, the muzzling word, and the echo in the word for the report.

Take Capernaum for his settled home from this point; note that the word for a spirit is never used in a good sense by the inspired writers; explain that the convulsion was permitted but the injury was not; connect the devil’s confession with what he had dared to claim in the wilderness; and admire the metaphor in the word for the spreading report.
Take the hearing of preaching as itself an act of worship and proper sabbath work, and find weight in every word spoken.

debates: Why Capernaum was chosen — as an act of mercy despite the rejection (Ambrose, Cyril) or simply as the new headquarters after Nazareth refused him (Robertson, Clarke, Wesley).
What “a spirit of an unclean devil” means, and whether the unusual phrase points to a particular class of spirit (Lightfoot) or is only Luke’s own combination (Robertson).

Why the devil confessed at all — because he could not endure the presence (Cyril), to steal the dignity of the confession from the Apostles (Chrysostom), from terror, or to make the character suspected (Wesley).
What the sabbath setting signifies, which Ambrose alone makes into an argument that the Son of God stands above the Law.
outliers: Ambrose alone reads the day of the healing as the opening of a new creation.
Wesley alone measures the devil’s present knowledge against his boast in the wilderness.
Tertullian alone is arguing about the dating of the descent rather than about the exorcism.
Robertson alone credits the untouched man to Luke’s eye as a physician.

38.pericope_label: Simon\u2019s wife\u2019s mother healed, and the sick brought at sunset

schools.summary: Explain the order of the two cures by the order of creation, the man healed first because first made; and observe that Christ heals both on request and unasked, always granting the prayer of the faithful and forgiving what they do not understand in themselves.

Take the rebuking of the fever as a figure of command addressed to a being that obeys; and give two reasons for the hour at which the sick were brought, the day’s employments or the belief that healing on the sabbath was unlawful.
Defend the same manner of speaking by making diseases and calamities God’s heralds, sent and recalled at his pleasure; and note that the demons came out unwillingly and at command.

Refuse the personification: the posture is a physician’s, not an exorcist’s, and Luke gives the look where the others give the touch; add the practical reasons for the sunset crowd, and note that the confession here is more definite as to the deity than the earlier one.
Mark the zeal of a crowd that would not wait for morning; and set the Jews’ denial of Christ against the devils’ confession.
Explain the hour by the close of the sabbath, and draw from Peter’s household the rule that acquaintance with good men brings blessings on a family.

debates: Whether the rebuking of the fever implies a personal agent — Origen and Calvin defend the personification on different grounds, Robertson denies it outright and makes the scene a physician’s.
Why the sick were brought only at sunset: the day’s occupations, scruple about healing on the sabbath, the cool of the evening, or the spread of the news.
Why the woman’s cure follows the man’s, which Ambrose alone explains from the order of creation.
What the demons’ confession adds to the earlier one, Robertson finding it a more definite statement of deity.
outliers: Robertson alone rejects the exorcistic reading of the rebuke and substitutes a bedside manner.
Calvin alone systematises the personification by making diseases God’s officers.
Cyril of Jerusalem alone sets the denial of the Jews against the confession of the devils as a pair.

42.pericope_label: He departs to a desert place, and preaches in the synagogues of Galilee

schools.summary: Explain the departure by the working of the miracles themselves, which are thought greater once the worker has gone and then speak with a voice of their own; and set the offence of the Pharisees at his power against the assent of the people to his words.

Prefer the stronger reading of the verb for seeking and take the eagerness as evidence of a people who had tasted the good word; and subordinate the healings to the preaching, as an emblematical and secondary work proving the authority to proclaim the kingdom.

Correct the English of the verb, which means to declare glad tidings rather than to preach, and note that the object is the other cities specifically; read the clause as a refusal of favouritism and the reason given as having a Johannine ring; and make the final verb a continuous imperfect describing a first tour.
Keep to the plain sense: the pursuit was on the following day, and the preaching was in the several synagogues of the towns throughout Galilee.

debates: Why he left while the crowd was still willing — because miracles work better in the worker’s absence (Chrysostom), or because the commission was to all the cities and not to a favoured few (Robertson).
Which reading of the verb for seeking is right, and what the eagerness proves (Clarke).
How preaching and healing stand to each other, Clarke making the miracles secondary and emblematical where Chrysostom credits them with a voice of their own.
What “I must preach” actually says, Ellicott distinguishing the verb from the ordinary word for preaching.
outliers: Chrysostom alone explains the withdrawal by the effect absence has on the reputation of a miracle.
Clarke alone argues a textual variant here, and alone ranks the healings expressly below the preaching.
Ellicott alone insists on the definite article before “other cities”.
Robertson alone reconstructs the night before from the other Gospel.
